doc.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Seville crowds, Louella Parsons and outdrawing Basie's band
summary: Packed houses, movie stars and low pay; the band outdrew Basie's at the Crescendo, and Wally Heider was auditioned for recording.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: She was and old time movie columnist who could make you or break you, you know, in the movie business. She’d be sitting there. It didn’t make any sense that people were coming to see the band. And we were the heroes. We played — $15 a night and our bar tabs were $23. You’ve got to be an idiot to do that. We were having so much fun. We didn’t care about the music. And that went on for about five weeks in a row. It was Mondays, maybe two nights a week. Then the club owner says, “Why don’t we do this five nights a week starting —” I said, “You really want to try it?” “Yeah,” he said, “let’s do it.” In the meantime I didn’t realize that Count Basie was opening right down about two blocks down in the place called the Crescendo. Now it’s a hard thing to say but we got scared. But we outdrew Basie’s band to a point where his band was in our club every time they had intermission, they were all there. They didn’t believe the band. Nobody did. I mean it was one of these things that, they were such a hit then but then again, once again, after I gave up the band in 1962, that was the end of that. And Buddy Rich and Shorty Rogers would come up to my house. See I had these tapes. When I recorded the band actually for records, Wally Heider had recorded the band, I’d auditioned Wally Heider at The Seville. I’d heard about him and I wanted to hear what he did. So he came in the club and he recorded the band, because I wanted to do a live album.
